design.title: Paired-survey batches: every training step sees the same places in all three photographs, not one photograph at a time
design.eli5: We handed the model three different aerial photographs of Berlin so it would learn the city rather than one picture of it — but the training routine showed it the whole first photo, then the whole second, then the whole third, like cramming three textbooks one after another the night before an exam. By the time it finished the third it had forgotten the first two, and the test (a fourth photo it has never seen) went badly. This experiment shuffles the three photos together so that every single study session shows the same street corners in all three photographs side by side. That forces it to notice what stays the same between the photos — the roads, the building shapes — instead of memorising the exact colours of one of them.
design.hypothesis: The baseline (experiment 1) did not learn three photographs — it learned one. Its train_capture_diagnostics read 0.015 on truedop_2023 (99% usable) but 1.401 on truedop_2022 and 1.533 on bb_dop20, i.e. the two other TRAINING photographs score almost as badly as the held-out one (1.651). The cause is in model/train.py: each epoch runs `for img in imgs:` with a complete 72,712-position lattice pass per photograph, so the model fits bb_dop20, then overwrites it with truedop_2022, then overwrites that with truedop_2023 — within-epoch catastrophic forgetting, with the cosine schedule ending on the 2023 pass. The shared trunk never receives a gradient that says 'these three different-looking crops are the SAME place' at the same time; it only ever receives 'this crop is cell k' from one survey at a time, which is exactly the single-photograph pixel-fingerprint regime the era was opened to escape. The limiting factor on the 2024 score is therefore not yet any invariance mechanism — it is that the three-survey training signal the era provides is not actually being applied. Building every batch from the same lattice positions extracted from all three photographs (same heading, same cell label) applies that signal directly: within one optimizer step the trunk is pushed to produce one cell-belief from three exposures of one place, which penalises features that only hold in one survey and rewards the structure (roads, building footprints, block layout) that all three share. Whether 3 MB of weights is still enough to store three separate fingerprints per cell instead is the open question this experiment makes measurable for the first time — the current baseline cannot answer it because it never tried to hold three.
